items.prompt: Black to move. Black is a knight for a pawn ahead. Find a move that keeps that advantage safe.

claims.statement: The engine (depth 16) rates Bg4 best, with Kg8 and c5 each within about two thirds of a pawn of it.
After Bg4 exactly one black piece, the bishop, attacks the knight on f3.
Bd5 scores at least 60 centipawns worse than the best move.

hints: Both the king on f7 and the bishop on e6 stand where White's pieces can attack them. Which move removes a target or creates one?
Three moves score best. One puts the bishop on a diagonal that attacks a white piece; one puts the king on the back rank; one is a pawn move that strikes at the centre.
Bg4, Kg8 or c5.
items.explain: Bg4 attacks the knight on f3, the piece that wants to jump to e5 with check. Kg8 takes the king off f7, where those checks arrive. c5 strikes at the d4 pawn at once. All three keep the extra piece. g6 and Qa5 also keep a lead but fall about three quarters of a pawn or more behind. Bd5 looks natural but lets the knight jump to e5 with check at once; at depth 16 it scores at least 60 centipawns worse than the best move.

feedback_by_move.e6d5: Bd5 lets the knight jump to e5 with check at once, and only one black piece can take it. It scores at least 60 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
feedback_by_move.g7g6: g6 also keeps Black ahead, but roughly three quarters of a pawn behind Bg4 at depth 16; the three best moves are Bg4, Kg8 and c5.

items.prompt: Black is in check from the knight on e5. Find the reply that keeps the most.

claims.statement: The engine (depth 16) rates Kg8 as the best reply.
Nxe5 scores at least 50 centipawns worse than the best reply.
After Nxe5 and dxe5 a white pawn attacks the knight on f6.
Ke8 loses by force (a mating line).

hints: Black can capture the knight, step to g8, or step to e8 or e6. Which of those leaves a white pawn with a free hit afterwards?
Capturing on e5 lets the pawn from d4 recapture with a gain of time on the knight on f6.
Kg8.
items.explain: Nxe5 dxe5 puts a white pawn on e5 attacking the knight on f6, so Black must spend a move on it. Kg8 steps out of check and leaves the knight on e5 where the knight on d7 still watches it. At depth 16 Nxe5 scores at least 50 centipawns worse than Kg8, and Ke8 loses by force.

feedback_by_move.d7e5: Nxe5 dxe5 attacks the knight on f6 with a pawn, which costs Black a move. It scores at least 50 centipawns worse than Kg8 (depth 16).
feedback_by_move.f7e8: Ke8 walks into a forced loss: the bishop checks on g6 and the position collapses (the engine finds a forced mate).

items.prompt: Black to move after 10.Re1, with the king on g8. The bishop on e6 has three sensible squares. Find the one the engine prefers.

claims.statement: The engine (depth 16) rates Bf7 as the best move.
Bd5 scores at least 60 centipawns worse than Bf7.
Bg4 scores at least 60 centipawns worse than Bf7.
On f7 the bishop attacks g6 and h5 as well as the diagonal back to a2.
On d5 the bishop attacks neither g6 nor h5.
The knight on f3 is defended twice, by the queen and the g2 pawn.

hints: The bishop can go to d5, g4 or f7. Which of those squares is next to the king?
From f7 the bishop covers the squares g6 and h5, where White's bishop and queen may want to land [H].
Bf7.
items.explain: On f7 the bishop stays beside the king and covers g6 and h5, squares where White's bishop and queen may want to land [H]; on d5 it covers neither. On g4 it attacks a knight that is defended twice. At depth 16 the engine rates Bf7 clearly best, and both Bd5 and Bg4 score at least 60 centipawns worse.

feedback_by_move.e6d5: Bd5 gives White the knight jump to e5 and leaves g6 and h5 uncovered. It scores at least 60 centipawns worse than Bf7 (depth 16).
feedback_by_move.e6g4: Bg4 attacks a knight that is defended twice, by the queen and the g2 pawn. It scores at least 60 centipawns worse than Bf7 (depth 16).

items.prompt: Black to move and already winning. Find the move that attacks the white queen with a rook that two black pieces defend.

claims.statement: The engine (depth 16) rates Rh5 as the best move.
After Rh5 the rook attacks the queen on g5.
After Rh5 two black pieces, the knight on f6 and the bishop on e8, defend the rook.

hints: Look at the fifth rank and at the white queen, defended only by the pawn on f4. Which black rook move attacks it?
A rook on h5 would attack the queen. Who defends the rook there?
Rh5.
items.explain: Rh5 attacks the queen on g5, which only the pawn on f4 defends. If the queen takes the rook, the knight on f6 or the bishop on e8 recaptures and White has given a queen for a rook; if the queen stays, Rxg5 fxg5 does the same. So the queen must leave, and Black keeps the attack. At depth 16 Rh5 is the engine's best move. Other moves such as Qd8 or Bb4 also keep Black winning, about half a pawn behind, but they do not attack the queen; this item asks for the rook that does.

feedback_by_move.h8h6: Rh6 keeps Black winning but does not attack the queen on g5; look for the rook move that does, with two defenders behind it.

items.prompt: Black to move. Find a move that keeps a lead for Black.

claims.statement: The engine (depth 16) rates all seven of these moves within 120 centipawns of the best move.
Bd6 scores at least 150 centipawns worse than the best move.
Two white pieces, the rook on e1 and the bishop on c4, attack the pawn on e6.

hints: The pawn on e6 is attacked twice, by the rook on e1 and the bishop on c4. How many black pieces defend it, and what happens if a defender is taken away?
A developing move that does nothing for the pawn on e6 allows a rook sacrifice there.
Qe8, Qa5, Nd5, b5, Na5, Ne7 or Nb4 keep an edge; Bd6 does not.
items.explain: The pawn on e6 is attacked by the rook and the bishop. Bd6 develops a piece but does nothing for e6, and Rxe6 starts a mating attack: it happened in two of the three games that reached this position (Shafer and Kowalski Rubiales), and White won both. Most good moves add a defender or hit an attacker: Qe8 and Ne7 attack the knight on g6, b5 and Na5 attack the bishop, Qa5 attacks the rook, Nd5 blocks the bishop. Nb4 passes the same engine test. At depth 16 these seven moves score within 120 centipawns of the best; Qd6, d3 and Qd7 keep a smaller lead and fall outside that margin, and Bd6 scores at least 150 worse.

feedback_by_move.f8d6: Bd6 allows Rxe6 followed by a mating attack (it happened in two games). It scores at least 150 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).

items.prompt: White to move after Black recaptured with the queen. Find the best move.

claims.statement: The engine (depth 16) rates Bg6+ as the best move.
h3 scores at least 400 centipawns worse than Bg6+.
After Bg6+ one white piece, the queen on c2, defends the bishop.
The engine (depth 16) rates this position slightly in White's favour, by between 0.1 and 1.5 pawns.
After Bg6+ only one black piece, the king, attacks the bishop on g6.

hints: The black queen on f4 is attacked by nothing yet. Which White move could gain a tempo by giving check?
The bishop on e4 can check the king from g6. Count who attacks g6 and who defends it.
Bg6+.
items.explain: After the queen recapture the engine prefers White, so Black's advantage is gone. Bg6+ is check; only the king attacks the bishop on g6, and the queen on c2 defends it, so the king cannot take. With the queen on f4 nothing else covers g6, and White gains the time that the move in the game, h3, threw away. At depth 16 Bg6+ is the engine's choice; h3 scores at least 400 centipawns worse.

feedback_by_move.h2h3: h3 attacks the bishop on g4, but Black simply trades on f3 and keeps a large advantage. It scores at least 400 centipawns worse than Bg6+ (depth 16).

items.prompt: Rewind one move. Black to move after White's bishop took the knight on f4. Find the recapture that keeps the advantage and avoids the check you just found.

claims.statement: The engine (depth 16) rates Bxf4 as the best move.
Qxf4 scores at least 300 centipawns worse than Bxf4.
After Qxf4 and Bg6+, one white piece, the queen on c2, defends the bishop on g6.
After Bxf4 and Bg6+, two black pieces, the queen on f6 and the king, attack the bishop on g6.

hints: Two black pieces can recapture on f4. After either, count how many black pieces attack g6 and how many white pieces defend a bishop landing there.
After the queen recaptures, the white bishop can move with check, and the queen behind it defends the bishop.
Bxf4.
items.explain: With the queen on f6 the bishop landing on g6 is attacked twice (queen and king) and defended once (queen on c2), so Bg6+ fails. After Qxf4 the queen has left the f6 square, only the king attacks g6, the queen on c2 defends it, the king cannot take, and White gains time. At depth 16 Bxf4 is the best move and Qxf4 scores at least 300 centipawns worse.

feedback_by_move.f6f4: Qxf4 allows Bg6+, protected by the queen on c2, with a gain of time. It scores at least 300 centipawns worse than Bxf4 (depth 16).

items.prompt: Black to move after 7.Nf3. White threatens a knight jump to e5 with check. Find the king move that makes that jump harmless.

claims.statement: After Kg8 the engine (depth 16) still rates Black ahead by between 0.5 and 2.6 pawns.
The king may step to g8.
The idle move a6 scores at least 100 centipawns worse than the best move.

hints: The knight jump would be check because the king stands on f7. Which square takes the king out of reach of the knight on e5?
The king has a square on the back rank next to the rook.
Kg8.
items.explain: On g8 the king is no longer on f7, so the knight jump to e5 is no longer a check (a bishop on c4 can still check along the diagonal). At depth 16 Black stays clearly ahead after Kg8, while an idle move such as a6 scores at least a pawn worse than the best move. Other developing moves are also fine; this item asks for the king move.

feedback_by_move.a7a6: a6 does nothing about the king. It scores at least 100 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
